explainBack.question: Why would an AI trained on ordinary preserved (FFPE) slides do worse on frozen sections than CRISP, even if it is excellent on preserved tissue?
explainBack.answer: Freezing, rapid slicing, and staining under time pressure change how the tissue physically looks compared with chemical-and-wax preservation. An FFPE-trained model learned visual patterns from a different-looking distribution of images, so frozen-section morphology falls partly outside what it has seen and its predictions degrade. CRISP was pretrained on frozen-section images specifically, so the appearance it encounters mid-surgery matches its training distribution.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: The article's statements that frozen preparation gives tissue a different appearance (P002) and that most existing AI learned from preserved slides while CRISP was trained for frozen images (P003), matching the paper's claim that FFPE specimens differ fundamentally in preparation and morphology.
explainBack.assessment: The article supplies exactly the causal chain needed for this answer in ordinary language; a reader could reproduce it from P002–P003 without outside knowledge.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A clinic director reads that a skin-lesion AI, trained on high-quality dermatoscope photos, 'matched board-certified dermatologists' in a reader study, and is asked whether to deploy it on smartphone photos patients upload from home.
unseenTransfer.question: Using this article's mechanism, what two problems should the director flag before treating the result as evidence the tool will improve care at her clinic?
unseenTransfer.answer: First, a training-distribution mismatch: like FFPE-trained models on frozen tissue, an AI trained on dermatoscope images may degrade on smartphone photos, which look different (lighting, focus, scale), so the matched-performance claim may not carry over. Second, evidence-type limits: matching specialists in a reader study is an observed-performance result under the tested conditions; it does not show patients end up better off. That requires an interventional study that changes care decisions and follows patient outcomes, just as the CRISP authors say they still need.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: P003's account of appearance mismatch between training and deployment images, and P005/P007's distinction between observed performance under tested conditions and proof of improved care.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The transfer holds cleanly: both the data-distribution logic and the observational-versus-interventional boundary apply directly to a scenario absent from the article.

frozen-specific.reason: Paper (p.12) states most existing foundation models are built on FFPE specimens which differ fundamentally from frozen sections in preparation and morphology, and CRISP was pretrained on frozen-section images specifically — matching the article's claim exactly.

result.reason: Paper reports consistent superiority over competing foundation models across independent prospective external cohorts, and the reader study found the senior pathologist's operating point fell on CRISP's ROC curve, i.e., comparable overall performance — matching 'beat other AI models' and 'matched the senior specialist overall'.

simulation-limit.reason: Paper (pp.13, 20, 34) describes a simulated deployment analysis on 100 consecutive SYCC cases estimating end-to-end timing (196.4s vs 292.6s), an observational not interventional design, and states a fully prospective interventional study is still necessary to assess impact on clinical outcomes (pp.23–24).
